comments.author: @SlowMonoxide
comments.text: I feel the same way about this as I have about every other image/video generation program. Is it technically impressive, and a sign that there may well come useful tools in the future? Yes. Is it, right now, a useful tool, or even a true prototype of a useful tool? No. It is, at best, a prototype of a component of a useful tool, which will require other components that work in fundamentally different ways. It can not follow basic instructions. In the muscle car video, it completely ignored the portions of the prompt about lighting. There were no neon lights in the cityscape, the car did not leave light trails as it drifted, and there was basically no use of lens flare, let alone the dramatic lens flare as it slid out of the last turn as explicitly specified in the prompt. In the hotpot video, instead of meatballs, it clearly rendered matzo balls, (or a similar style of psuedo-dumpling) etc. It is apparent that these image/video generation models are held back by the same problem as textual LLMs, i.e. that they do not parse the meaning of the prompt and then attempt to comply, but rather are assembling probabilities based on the data they have seen in the past. They do not 'understand' the prompt as a whole, they are merely matching individual bits of it to different probability spaces and Frankensteining the individual elements together in ways that are, again, based on probabilistic assessment of how elements they have seen before have been arranged. I'd like to reiterate that this process is, itself, quite technically impressive, but it fundamentally is not what it is advertised as. These types of models may form an important component of yet to be developed actually useful tools, but are not likely to become said tools themselves. While continually refining this type of component is not a bad thing, and in fact is quite necessary, it will never lead to the qualitative change needed for the next step. The addition of components with fundamentally different mechanics is absolutely necessary for 'more intelligent' programs to be a thing. The pale imitation we can form with merely the small pool of current techniques will never close that gap alone.

Size and Age: Juvenile capybaras are definitely vulnerable, and crocodiles will prey on them. However, adult capybaras are quite large (the largest rodents in the world!), often reaching over 100 pounds. This size difference can make them a challenging and risky prey for smaller crocodiles.

Capybaras' Behavior: Capybaras are highly social and live in large groups. There's safety in numbers. They are also adept swimmers and can quickly escape into the water, which is their preferred escape route when threatened. They're also surprisingly fast on land.

Habitat Overlap, Not Constant Interaction: While both species inhabit similar wetland areas, they don't necessarily interact all the time. Capybaras often graze in open areas while crocodiles tend to lurk in the water. This separation in time and space reduces the frequency of encounters.

Dietary Preferences: Crocodiles are opportunistic predators, but their primary diet consists of fish, turtles, snakes, and birds. While they will take larger mammals if the opportunity arises, it's not their main focus. An adult capybara is a substantial meal that requires significant effort.
